sources.news_title: Hackers hit top financial platforms — users suffer staggering losses
sources.text:
The prediction market and cryptocurrency leaders each vow to make the victims whole.
Two popular financial platforms came under attack Thursday within hours of each other. The cryptocurrency platform Binance and prediction market platform Polymarket both suffered huge losses totaling billions of dollars, and it was all stolen directly from users’ accounts.
Both platforms are juggernauts in their categories. Binance is by far the biggest cryptocurrency exchange on the planet, boasting 335 million users, which makes it a prime target for hackers. Meanwhile, Polymarket is the leading prediction market, edging out Kalshi for global dominance.
Binance revealed that it set aside $6.34 billion to recuperate the losses suffered by its users.
Binance was the first to take a hit. According to an official post sent out by the company’s X account:
Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. User funds are completely safe.
Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information.
Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.
Unfortunately, the claim that user funds were safe and secure quickly fell apart. In the next 24 hours, Binance revealed that it set aside $6.34 billion to recuperate the losses suffered by its users, all of which Binance vows to pay back in full.
Users can currently deposit money into their Binance accounts, but withdrawals are paused as the company works with law enforcement and blockchain experts to investigate the attack. So far, they know it is linked to TraderTraitor, a hacking group based in North Korea.
RELATED: Another major AI attack hits the internet — this time targeting the backbone of American capitalism
Black_Kira//Getty Images
Around the same time, Polymarket was hacked, with bad actors siphoning $2.7 million from 737 users’ accounts. The attack was made possible through a vulnerability in a third-party system that allowed the attackers to intervene in active trading sessions and take funds.
Just like Binance, Polymarket has vowed to repay the affected users. Trading on Polymarket was halted temporarily while the issue was resolved. All systems are now back online.
Although the Polymarket story may be over, the Binance debacle is still developing, even as it closes out a tumultuous Black October. Blaze News will have an update on the latest early next week as more details unfold.

sources.news_title: $6.3 billion stolen in biggest cryptocurrency heist in history
sources.text:
$6.3 billion stolen in biggest cryptocurrency heist in history
By Molly Grace • Published: 30 Oct 2026 • 23:20 • 4 minutes read
North Korean-linked groups have been accused of stealing digital currencies. Photo credit: JOCA_PH/Shutterstock
Imagine checking your cryptocurrency account and discovering that the exchange holding your money has been hit by a theft worth billions. That is the situation facing Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, after hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion in a cyberattack that has sent shockwaves through the cryptocurrency industry. The attack took place on Thursday, October 29, targeting the systems Binance uses to authorise and process transactions.
The theft is being described as the largest cryptocurrency heist in history, with blockchain analysts reporting that much of the money was transferred within approximately 20 minutes. Binance has pledged to cover the full financial loss, but the scale of the breach has raised serious questions about how an exchange handling billions of dollars in digital assets could have its security systems compromised.
Hackers exploited Binance’s transaction systems
Binance’s initial investigation suggested that the attack may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The hackers are believed to have used access gained through the device to enter a service container and submit withdrawal transactions without proper authorisation. The company later discovered additional points of compromise and said the incident was more complex than first understood. It has not yet published a complete technical explanation of how the attackers managed to move such a large amount of cryptocurrency.
Investigators believe the attackers gained control of part of the infrastructure responsible for approving transactions. This allowed them to authorise transfers to wallets under their control. Binance has said there is currently no evidence that private keys belonging to its wallets were leaked. It has revoked the affected authorisations and is examining the systems involved in the breach.
Binance promises to replace the stolen money
The exchange has said it will absorb the entire financial impact rather than pass the losses on to users. It is using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), an emergency reserve established to protect customers in the event of serious security incidents, alongside its corporate funds. In its October 30 update, Binance said it had allocated more than $6.34 billion to cover the loss. Around $5 billion was held in the same types of cryptocurrency that had been stolen, with the remaining amount being purchased through market and over-the-counter transactions.
The company said it had already covered approximately 80 per cent of the affected amount. That commitment is significant given the size of the theft. The amount involved is far beyond the losses suffered in many previous cryptocurrency exchange attacks, and replacing it requires Binance to put substantial company resources behind its promise.
Billions frozen as investigators trace the money
Recovering the stolen cryptocurrency is another matter. Once digital assets have been transferred between wallets, tracing their movements can be difficult, particularly when criminals use multiple addresses and services in an attempt to conceal where the funds have gone. Binance reported that approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen through cooperation with its partners. The company is also working with law enforcement agencies, blockchain intelligence firms and cryptocurrency issuers to identify and restrict further transfers.
Tether and Circle are among the companies reported to have frozen assets connected to the incident. Their involvement is important because issuers of certain digital currencies can sometimes freeze tokens held at identified wallet addresses. However, freezing assets does not mean that all the stolen money has been recovered. The whereabouts of the remaining funds are still being investigated, and the final amount that can be retrieved remains uncertain.
North Korean hackers suspected
Attention has also turned to the possible identity of those behind the attack. Blockchain analysis firms have identified similarities between the Binance incident and previous cryptocurrency thefts linked to North Korean hacking groups. Researchers at TRM Labs and other firms have pointed to techniques resembling those used in earlier attacks, including the major theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in 2025.
North Korean-linked groups have been accused of stealing digital currencies to generate funds for the country. However, no official investigation has publicly confirmed that North Korea was responsible for the Binance breach, and the suspected connection remains under examination.
Withdrawals suspended while security checks continue
Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while it investigated the breach and secured the affected systems. The exchange subsequently said that deposits and services not affected by the attack remained operational, although withdrawals were still subject to security checks before normal access could resume. The company has been working to strengthen its transaction approval systems and verify that the breach has been contained. It has also promised to release a more detailed technical account once its investigation is complete.
The attack has also affected confidence across the cryptocurrency market. Bitcoin and Ether came under pressure following reports of the theft, while shares in some companies connected to the digital currency industry also fell. Binance now faces questions over how hackers managed to breach its transaction systems and whether its security measures are strong enough to prevent another attack Even if the company makes good on every dollar, the breach has exposed how vulnerable an exchange can be when attackers find a way into the machinery used to approve transactions. And with $6.3 billion involved, the questions about how it happened are unlikely to disappear when the money is replaced.

$6 billion stolen from world’s largest crypto exchange
(CNN)– The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suspended withdrawals after being hacked.
Binance said Thursday night, October 29, the hackers went through an engineer’s laptop to break into its digital wallets and steal $6 billion.
It appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever.
According to multiple crypto-tracing firms, evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea.
A team of cryptocurrency firms managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot.
Binance said user funds are safe, and it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund.

sources.news_title: How Hackers Drained $6.36 Billion From Binance in Just Twenty Minutes
sources.text:
Imagine losing over six billion dollars in the time it takes to eat lunch. That nightmare became reality for Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, on October 29, 2026. Starting at 20:05 UTC, attackers launched a blitz across the digital financial world. They drained approximately $6.36 billion from Binance wallets across ten different blockchains. Most of that staggering sum vanished in just twenty minutes. Crypto analysts immediately called it the largest cyber heist in history. The theft is roughly four times larger than the $1.5 billion Bybit hack from February 2025.
How did the thieves pull off such a massive operation so quickly? Initial reports pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a Binance engineer. That breach reportedly gave attackers access to a service container to submit unauthorized withdrawals. However, Binance executives later clarified that the attack was far more complex than a single click. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs noted that the hackers compromised Binance’s hot wallet signing infrastructure. On the Ethereum network, the attackers used fifty pre-signed authorizations prepared in advance. They turned a Binance hot wallet into an automated sweeper under their direct control. Meanwhile, wallets on nine other blockchains sent funds through ordinary signed transfers. Ethereum accounted for $3.79 billion of the haul, while Bitcoin outflows reached $1.47 billion. Millions more poured out from Tron, Solana, Arbitrum, and the XRP Ledger.
Intelligence experts quickly spotted familiar fingerprints on the digital crime scene. Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis attributed the attack with high confidence to North Korea. Specifically, they named an elite state-sponsored hacking unit known as TraderTraitor. This group operates as part of North Korea’s notorious Lazarus Group. Officials say the heavily sanctioned regime uses crypto thefts to fund its economy and nuclear weapons program.
A frantic digital chase began within hours of the breach. Binance suspended withdrawals to run security checks and promised to cover all user losses. Major blockchain networks and stablecoin issuers stepped in to help stop the bleeding. Tether, Circle, Ripple, World Liberty Financial, and Arbitrum froze roughly $2.7 billion in stolen assets. Still, the hackers raced ahead by swapping tokens and borrowing assets on decentralized platforms. They currently hold about $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum beyond any central authority’s reach. Even after the freezes, their remaining haul shatters every previous theft record.

sources.news_title: The World’s Biggest Crypto Heist
sources.text:
The World’s Biggest Crypto Heist
Suspected North Korean hackers stole $6.36 billion in digital coins from Binance.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an alleged North Korean cyberattack on Binance, Israel’s parliamentary election results, and mixed NATO messaging on Russia’s threat to Europe.
$6.36 Billion in 20 Minutes
Hackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange late Thursday, stealing more than $6 billion in under 30 minutes. Experts are calling it the biggest crypto heist in history, and initial investigations suggest that North Korea is to blame.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an alleged North Korean cyberattack on Binance, Israel’s parliamentary election results, and mixed NATO messaging on Russia’s threat to Europe.
$6.36 Billion in 20 Minutes
Hackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange late Thursday, stealing more than $6 billion in under 30 minutes. Experts are calling it the biggest crypto heist in history, and initial investigations suggest that North Korea is to blame.
According to U.S.-based blockchain research firm TRM Labs, an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor targeted $6.36 billion in Binance digital coins spread across 10 blockchains. The hackers were unable to access consumer accounts, instead only affecting Binance corporate holdings. Around $3 billion in assets have already been located or frozen, but TRM Labs estimates that the hackers had moved roughly $2.4 billion in crypto coins “beyond any issuer’s reach.”
“Your assets are safe,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on Friday in a statement intended to ease customers’ concerns. However, analysts argue that the heist—despite its limited impact on consumers—has exposed the risks of trading crypto as well as the growing prowess of North Korean hacking efforts.
Cryptocurrency is a relatively new phenomenon in the world of economics—and one that is still largely unregulated. In June 2024, then-presidential candidate Donald Trump vowed to make the United States the “crypto capital of the planet” if elected for a second term, and since then, he has focused on reducing aggressive oversight of the lucrative industry. He also launched his own cryptocurrency platform, World Liberty Financial, which is run by his two sons, as well his own meme coin cryptocurrency.
Some countries, such as Russia, have turned to cryptocurrency to help evade sanctions and procure sensitive dual-use goods. Crypto companies have also faced a slew of cyberattacks. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency accused North Korean hackers of stealing roughly $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the course of five years. Such hackers came under scrutiny again in February 2025, when the FBI said that TraderTraitor stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, one of Binance’s top rivals. And last month, attackers took around $350 million from cryptocurrency exchange Bitget.
A Binance spokesperson told The Associated Press on Friday that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.” However, TRM Labs said that its analysts had “high confidence” in the company’s assessment that the North Korean hacking group is responsible.
“North Korean hackers are among the world’s most aggressive and highly skilled cyber actors,” former South Korean Vice Defense Minister Shin Beom-chul told the Financial Times on Friday. Last year alone, Pyongyang’s hackers stole around $2 billion in cryptocurrency, accounting for roughly 60 percent of total crypto heists in the world, according to estimates from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.
Bitcoin’s value plummeted more than 5 percent overnight Thursday into Friday in response to the Binance heist, and other cryptocurrency exchanges dropped as much as 9 percent.
Today’s Most Read
- No One Has a Plan for American Decline by Nick Danforth
- In Deadlocked Israeli Election, Netanyahu Has Upper Hand by David E. Rosenberg
- Dawn of the Data Centers by Christina Lu
What We’re Following
Israel’s coalition talks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have lost their parliamentary majority, final election results confirmed on Friday. Although Netanyahu’s Likud bloc still has the most seats in the Knesset, a historic showing by unaligned Arab parties means that lawmakers likely have several weeks of intense coalition-building negotiations ahead of them before a new government can be formed. In the interim, Netanyahu remains in charge.
According to the final results, Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc won 53 seats, main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party-led alliance won 48 seats, and Arab-led groups won a record 19 seats. If Eisenkot wants to dethrone Netanyahu, then he will likely need to ally with the Arab parties to secure a majority. However, Eisenkot may be loath to do so, as one of his key partners, right-wing lawmaker Avigdor Lieberman, has ruled out joining a coalition with the predominately Arab Joint List or Raam parties.
Netanyahu has capitalized on such hesitance, accusing Qatar of funneling money into Israel to support the Arab vote. Israel’s elections committee said the “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless,” and the Qatari government dismissed Netanyahu’s accusations as “ridiculous and dangerous.” Yet Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has promised to investigate the claims.
Pentagon messaging on Moscow. The Trump administration has urged several NATO members in recent weeks to water down their rhetoric regarding the threat that Russia poses to Europe, Reuters reported on Friday. Sources said that senior U.S. defense officials, including Defense Department policy chief Elbridge Colby, have urged Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania to dial down their warnings, arguing that they are not helpful for ongoing peace talks. Russian hybrid warfare, including drone incursions, has hit all three NATO members in the past year.
U.S. negotiators are reportedly considering new incentives to end the Russia-Ukraine war, including possible sanctions relief for and business deals with Moscow. Last week, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff held separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin; during talks with Putin, Witkoff called the Russian leader a “humanitarian” and announced that negotiations would soon begin on the technical level.
The report about the Pentagon’s urgings also came on the same day as a G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attended in person. Deep rifts among the attendees prompted U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to cancel the group’s traditional family photo, as many participants balked at standing beside Lavrov. Several European leaders have accused the Trump administration of being too soft on Moscow.
Global port strike. Dockworkers in 22 countries went on strike on Friday to protest the use of ports for arms exports and, specifically, for the delivery of weapons to active war zones. More than 25 unions across 113 ports—from Southern Europe to North Africa and India—backed the protests, which are in support of the so-called Istanbul Declaration, a document signed in May by dockworker unions from more than 35 European ports that demands an end to arms shipments from their sites.
“From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and genocide,” unions said at a press conference held to announce the strike. The Global Sumud Flotilla, a pro-Palestinian maritime activist group that has repeatedly tried to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza to deliver humanitarian supplies, also vowed to support Friday’s movement.
It is unclear how disruptive the 24-hour demonstration might be. Organizers said that the strike could impact more than 40 percent of Mediterranean cargo and around $2 billion worth of freight. However, shipping experts suspect that global trade will not be significantly hurt. Still, FP energy reporter Keith Johnson told World Brief that the strike “is more sand in the gears of a global economy already strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade wars and real wars, both of which have sent freight rates to nosebleed levels this autumn.”
What in the World?
How did right-wing presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro react to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s runoff election victory on Sunday?
A. He graciously conceded defeat.
B. He called for his followers to protest his loss in Brasília.
C. He fled to Chile.
D. He said he would request an annulment of the election.
Odds and Ends
For a small sum of $56 million, you too can be the owner of a famous Impressionist painting. Claude Monet’s Iris became the most expensive artwork sold at auction in France last Thursday. The massive canvas, depicting some of Monet’s favorite flowers in his Giverny garden, is part of a 20-piece series produced near the end of the artist’s life. It took the title of most expensive work sold at a French auction from sculptor Amedeo Modigliani’s Head of a Caryatid, which sold for around $48 million in 2010.
And the Answer Is…
D. He said he would request an annulment of the election.
Lula became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in history to come from behind to win the election’s second round, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports. Bolsonaro, the subject of several criminal probes, subsequently fled to Miami, where he called himself “the leader of Brazil.”

sources.news_title: Crypto Was Supposed to Be Unhackable. So How Did North Korea Just Steal $6 Billion in 20 Minutes?
sources.text:
On Thursday, Binance—the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange—got to add another “world’s largest” accolade to its name by becoming the target of the biggest cryptocurrency heist in the industry’s history. According to the company, more than $6 billion in digital coins were stolen from users’ digital wallets. Binance has already announced that it’s restored some of the lost funds to affected accounts.
Although the details of the hack are still a bit fuzzy, TRM Labs, a crypto research company, says the money moved out of 10 blockchains within 20 minutes and attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, a hacking unit associated with North Korea. In February last year, the FBI traced a $1.5 billion hack of the crypto exchange Bybit to the same group. A smaller hack this April was also linked to the broader North Korean–run Lazarus Group.
In Thursday’s hack, TRM Labs reports that no specific cryptocurrency was safe, as digital coins were stolen from wallets containing Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana, and six others. The balances were sent to an account operated by the attacker. After news of the hack, Bitcoin's price dropped a few percentage points, though it stayed above its low from this past summer.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a post on X. “We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
One of the purported benefits of the blockchain is its inherent security, mostly due to its decentralized nature, along with its strong cryptographic protocols. However, crypto exchanges are much more vulnerable than blockchain itself because they’re essentially a centralized holder of assets. They’re also prone to technical vulnerabilities, not least of which can be simple human error. In that same statement on X, Binance announced that its initial investigation found that a “compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop” may have allowed hackers to gain access to a service container—which they then used to make the withdrawals. However, Binance followed up that statement hours later, suggesting that the laptop may only be one vulnerability and that there were “additional points of breach.”
North Korea has targeted cryptocurrency exchanges since at least 2017, according to The Guardian, drawn by “the sector’s relatively lax security controls” and relatively weak regulatory oversight. Binance has faced its own regulatory problems. In 2023, founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to violating the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program, and the company agreed to pay more than $4 billion in penalties. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025.
As for North Korea, when it comes to crypto hacking—business is booming. A United Nations (UN) panel concluded in 2024 that these types of hacks accounted for roughly half of the reclusive country’s foreign currency income, and were a significant fundraiser for the country’s nuclear weapons program. Due to the decentralized, pseudonymous nature of cryptocurrencies, these funds also bypass international sanctions meant to rein in Pyongyang’s most bellicose impulses.
Now, it appears that North Korea has scored its biggest windfall yet.

sources.news_title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
sources.text:
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack.
“We are working nonstop to resolve this,” Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: “We’re looking at that.”
Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
North Korean hackers are suspected in the attack
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”
U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. “Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record
While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn’t recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst.
“Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler,” he said. “You mix it in with other cryptos, and it’s harder to track.”
How long it will take the hackers to turn that into something usable isn’t clear, he said. “The bottom line is there are places in the world where you can take your bitcoin and get that converted,” Hileman said.
TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor.
Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace.
“A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI,” said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. “Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines.”
Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong
The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
Teng, Binance’s co-CEO, confirmed in a nearly five-minute video posted on X Friday that Binance's own hot wallet was affected. “User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets” — which are offline and used for secure storage — “and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal.”
Teng said Binance's tech and security teams are “still deep” in investigating the hack. He said it was not carried out by one person and that the attackers used complex tactics, including a "self-destruct mechanism" that is making the incident more difficult to investigate.
“We are working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover stolen funds," Teng said. "We will do everything within our power to make sure that these bad actors will be held accountable.”
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.
___
Associated Press writers John Seewer and Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.
Kaitlyn Huamani And Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

sources.text:
Crypto exchange Binance suspended withdrawals after elite hackers stole a staggering $6.3 billion in digital assets, marking what may be the biggest crypto heist of all time.
Researchers at the crypto research firm TRM Labs told the New York Times that they have “high confidence” in its assessment that the theft was the work of “North Korea’s elite hacking unit.” It reportedly took just 20 minutes to drain Binance of billions of dollars in crypto.
Binance said that it was able to work with its partners to freeze about $3 billion in assets. TRM, however, estimates that around $2.4 billion in assets were moved “beyond any issuer’s reach,” per the NYT, meaning that those coins are likely as good as gone.
The exchange stated in an X-formerly-Twitter post that it had initially thought that the breach was the result of a single compromised employee laptop. Further investigation, however, suggests that the attack was more elaborate.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said. “We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them.”
The crypto firm also said that it would “cover all losses” using reserve funds.
Binance founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao said on X that “user funds are safe,” but the incident “does look like a hack.” Zhao, a major player in the crypto world, pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced to four months in prison in 2024 but was pardoned last year by president Donald Trump after Binance provided support to World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s much-scrutinized crypto venture. (Zhao is no longer Binance’s CEO, but is still a shareholder.)
Previously, crypto’s biggest heist was last February’s attack on Binance rival Bybit, according to NYT. That attack was also carried out by North Korean hackers, who made away with $1.5 billion. TRM told Reuters that the Bybit and Binance heists share similarities suggesting that the same team may be responsible for both breaches.
That North Korea is responsible once again is unsurprising: the isolated nation, which has been under the thumb of dictators for decades, relies heavily on state-sponsored crime to bring in cash.
Crypto has always been risky — and even riskier now that cybercriminals have access to advanced AI tools that are supercharging hacking efforts across the digital world.

sources.news_title: AI is rewriting the rules of cybersecurity. Who has the advantage?
sources.text:
AI is rewriting the rules of cybersecurity. Who has the advantage?
The $6.3 billion Binance cryptocurrency heist shows how AI is transforming cybersecurity, raising the stakes for hackers and defenders alike.
Late Thursday afternoon, suspected North Korean hackers pulled off the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. After breaching a single account at the giant crypto firm Binance and draining $2.5 billion, the hackers compromised 10 other accounts within a 12-minute window.
In all, they stole $6.3 billion, according to Binance.
It could have been worse. A security company called Blockaid, which uses advanced artificial intelligence, says it detected the initial break-in in less than two minutes and, within the hour, had alerted customers to the attack. The hackers did not get away with all the money. Other cryptocurrency companies were able to trace and freeze roughly $3 billion of what the hackers initially took, Binance said.
AI is making it easier for hackers to steal money, personal information, and passwords. That same technology is what banks and businesses are racing to use to shield consumers.
Welcome to cybersecurity in the age of AI.
Just as assembly lines revolutionized manufacturing, AI is transforming the contest between hackers and cybersecurity firms, allowing both sides to operate faster, on a larger scale, and with less human intervention. Though the Binance hack hasn’t been definitively traced to AI, the scale of the breach is shaking the world of finance even as concerns have surged about AI’s role in expanding the risks institutions face.
Software known as AI agents is quickly giving hackers the power to automate their attacks so that, with little or no human assistance, they can attack more targets and threaten everything from your bank account to your identity. Using the same tools, cybersecurity and AI companies are working ever faster to stay a step ahead and protect those things.
The winners will be companies and governments that adapt quickly to the new technology. The losers will be those that don’t.
“I can only hope that the rest of the world can understand it’s a matter of when [a cyberattack will happen], not if,” says Brandon Tirado, the vice president in charge of cybersecurity operations for ReliaQuest, a global cybersecurity firm based in Tampa, Florida.
During the first half of 2026, crypto companies lost some $1.1 billion in a record 212 verified hacking incidents, according to Blockaid. That was more than triple the attacks recorded in all of 2025.
What’s going on with AI and AI hacking?
On the positive side, AI agents are helping companies, as never before, find software vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them. Last week, for example, companies coordinated a fix for vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used on 70% of websites worldwide. Those vulnerabilities were exposed by agents this year and kept secret until the companies could devise a fix.
The rollout of the fix was bumpy because news of the vulnerabilities leaked out, Mr. Tirado says. Some companies and governments closed down websites to avoid any problems. Fortunately, the fix was apparently deployed before hackers could find the PHP vulnerabilities.
On the negative side, hackers can use the same “helping” AI agents to discover software vulnerabilities that they can then exploit.
Are there examples that shed light on the challenge?
In September, a Chinese hacking group known as Storm-0940 began using a “penetration-testing harness,” a suite of automated tools that cybersecurity firms use to find vulnerabilities. According to a Microsoft report last week, the group used this harness, or testing system, to automate attacks against hundreds of organizations worldwide across aerospace, defense, automotive, chemical, financial, and other industries, as well as against government agencies, think tanks, and nonprofits.
The harness also managed to gain access to several internet cloud-based systems, sometimes in as little as three hours.
In the ConnectWise attack this month, hackers used compromised application credentials to try to access more than 2,250 customer accounts. In a separate operation, they launched up to 2,900 login attempts per minute against Microsoft accounts. Those login attempts failed, but Microsoft found evidence that the attackers had meanwhile gained privileged access to other organizations’ cloud systems.
Cybersecurity firms believe Storm-0940 is aligned with China’s government, which has denied being aware of the incident.
Perhaps equally worrying is that AI’s expertise is enabling hackers with lower sophistication and far fewer resources to carry out similar attacks.
Last week, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike reported that a hacker with limited cybersecurity expertise used Anthropic’s Claude Code to compromise several Indonesian government websites, a government domain in another country, and several private-sector organizations.
“We expect over the next 12 months, some low-skill threat actors will likely use agentic AI to conduct campaigns at a level of effectiveness and scale previously only achievable by organized criminal groups or state-nexus actors,” the CrowdStrike report forecast.
Already, the average number of weekly cyberattacks in September rose 16% compared with August and 48% from a year ago, according to Check Point Research. While not all of those attacks involved AI, experts warn that the technology makes it easier for less-skilled hackers to target more organizations.
How can a company protect itself?
Take Bank of America. In the second quarter, the nation’s second-largest bank added 1,000 contractors to its existing 3,000-strong cybersecurity workforce to help plug its software vulnerabilities against AI-enabled hackers, the bank’s CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC recently. The bank spent more than $200 million during the third quarter on this work and anti-money-laundering compliance measures.
Such preemptive AI work could help protect firms – and their customers – from hackers.
“The companies that do that are going to be ahead of the game,” says V.S. Subrahmanian, a computer scientist at Northwestern University. “The companies that dither, dawdle, and don’t do that run the risk that the bad guys are going to get ahead of them.”
Whether AI agents have given hackers or defenders an advantage remains a subject of debate.
“Microsoft can amortize the cost of all that finding [of vulnerabilities] over its entire customer base, so it’s cheaper overall for the defender than the attacker,” says Bruce Schneier, a fellow at Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society and the author of more than a dozen books on AI, cybersecurity, and trust. “On the minus side, the defender is much slower. It is faster to find and exploit than it is to find and fix.”

sources.news_title: Biggest Crypto Heist Ever? Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion From Binance, North Korean Group Under Scanner
sources.text:
Biggest Crypto Heist Ever? Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion From Binance, North Korean Group Under Scanner
The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has suffered a major cyberattack in which hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from its wallets. The incident is being described as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
Binance confirmed the security breach on Thursday, October 29, and said it was working with law enforcement agencies, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to investigate the attack and trace the stolen funds.
The exchange initially suspected that a compromised employee laptop had played a role in the breach. However, a later investigation revealed additional points of compromise, suggesting that the attack was more complex than first believed.
Blockchain intelligence firms have pointed towards a North Korean hacking group as a possible suspect, although Binance and law enforcement agencies have not officially confirmed who was responsible.
Here is what happened, how the hackers reportedly carried out the attack and what it means for Binance users.
What Happened In The Binance Hack?
As per Binance and blockchain analytics firms, around $6.3 billion of cryptocurrencies were transferred from wallets utilized by Binance to process transactions.
The stolen cryptocurrency was distributed over a number of blockchain platforms. TRM Labs, a blockchain analytics company, indicated that the amount of about $6.36 billion had been transferred over 10 blockchains, with the majority of the hack occurring within 20 minutes on Thursday.
Binance stated the event as a sophisticated cyber-attack. In an announcement on X, the firm noted that it is working with law enforcement and partners in the industry to investigate the incident.
The exchange further cautioned that the amount reported might vary as further analysis would be carried out.
How Did Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion?
The initial findings of Binance were that attackers might have used a breached DevOps engineer's laptop to penetrate the system.
The report stated that this breach gave attackers access to a service container and permission for unauthorized withdrawals.
However, Binance later clarified that researchers found multiple other points where the breach occurred. Co-CEO Richard Teng stated that the attack involved a sophisticated process and was not just about an employee using their own permissions wrongly.
According to blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs, the attackers exploited Binance's signing infrastructure which helps to authorize the cryptocurrency transactions. This helped attackers give commands to empty the wallets.
Blockchain logs showed that most of the money stolen was moved in around 20 minutes.
Who Is Behind The Binance Cyberattack?
The identity of the hackers has not been officially confirmed by Binance or law enforcement agencies.
However, two major blockchain intelligence firms, TRM Labs and Chainalysis, have linked the attack to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor.
TRM Labs said it made the attribution with high confidence, while Chainalysis also described the attack as likely involving the same North Korean-linked group.
TraderTraitor has previously been associated with major cryptocurrency thefts. However, the latest attribution remains an assessment by blockchain intelligence firms and should not be treated as an officially confirmed finding.
What Will Happen To Binance Users' Money?
Following the attack, Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals and deposits as a precaution while it reviewed its security systems. The company later said deposits were operating normally, while withdrawals remained suspended during security checks.
Binance has assured customers that their funds are safe and pledged to cover all losses arising from the incident.
The exchange said it had reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to address the impact of the attack. This includes around $5 billion already held in the affected digital assets.
Binance is also working with blockchain companies, cryptocurrency issuers and other partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds. The exchange said approximately $3 billion worth of assets had been frozen.
Freezing cryptocurrency does not automatically mean the funds have been returned. However, it can prevent attackers from transferring or converting those assets through services that cooperate with investigators.
When Will Binance Withdrawals Resume?
Binance mentioned that they were trying to restore their withdrawal service following completion of their security checks and implementation of necessary changes to the compromised systems.
In its update dated October 30, Binance said that they would be able to resume their withdrawals within about 45 hours. It was their expected time and not an officially confirmed reopening time.
Furthermore, the company has mentioned that they will provide a comprehensive technical report at the conclusion of their investigation and also an updated proof of reserve once their security enhancements have been completed.
The investigation in relation to this cyber-attack is still ongoing as the company tries to track down the stolen cryptocurrencies and also determine how exactly this compromise took place.

sources.news_title: Estimated $6.3 billion stolen from Binance in the largest crypto heist ever recorded; nearly $3 billion has already been frozen
sources.text:
The Briefing
- Hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in the biggest digital asset theft ever recorded.
- Blockchain analytics firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both attribute the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite state-sponsored hacking unit.
- Binance pledged to cover all losses using more than $6.34 billion in reserved company funds; roughly $3 billion has already been frozen by stablecoin issuers and industry partners.
The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange was targeted in an operation that will redefine the boundaries of digital asset crime. On Thursday, attackers drained an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance across ten separate blockchains — a single breach that nearly doubled the total amount stolen from the entire crypto industry throughout all of 2025.
One Laptop, Ten Blockchains, Twenty Minutes
The entry point was deceptively simple. According to Binance's preliminary findings, a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop gave the attacker access to a service container, from which a wave of unauthorized withdrawal transactions was triggered. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs tracked approximately $6.36 billion leaving Binance's hot wallets across ten blockchains — with the overwhelming bulk of those transfers executed in roughly 20 minutes.
The operation was meticulously prepared. TRM Labs found evidence that the attackers began staging the heist at least 36 hours before striking, discreetly funding operator wallets through Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service designed to obscure transaction trails. Transaction signatures were obtained in advance, then released in one coordinated burst.
North Korea's Elite Hacking Unit in the Crosshairs
Two of the most respected names in blockchain forensics converged on the same suspect. TRM Labs attributed the breach with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the cryptocurrency-focused subunit of North Korea's Lazarus Group. Chainalysis co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin said his firm was "confident" in the same attribution, pointing to established laundering patterns and a critical on-chain discovery: stolen Binance funds commingled directly with assets taken in a separate Bitget breach the prior month — itself also tied to Pyongyang.
Binance noted in its public statement that several attack characteristics mirrored patterns seen in previous North Korea-linked operations, including the $1.5 billion theft from exchange Bybit in February 2025 — a breach the FBI formally attributed to TraderTraitor. The regime has increasingly turned to crypto heists as a primary channel for raising hard currency to fund its nuclear weapons development and sustain its isolated economy.
Industry Mobilizes: Nearly $3 Billion Frozen Within Hours
The cross-industry response that followed was both swift and unusually coordinated. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle together froze more than $2.3 billion in assets linked to the hackers' wallets. Ripple locked down roughly $200 million in additional funds. Binance confirmed that total frozen assets reached approximately $3 billion, though investigators cautioned the number remains subject to change as tracing work continues.
World Liberty Financial — a crypto venture associated with the family of U.S. President Donald Trump — also disclosed that it coordinated with digital asset custodian BitGo to freeze a portion of the stolen funds, illustrating how broadly the industry mobilized in the hours after the breach became public.
Binance Pledges Full Coverage, Halts Withdrawals
Despite the staggering scale of the breach, Binance was unequivocal: user funds are safe, and the exchange will absorb every dollar of the loss. The company pointed to more than $6.34 billion in reserved company funds to cover the incident. Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security teams audited the platform's infrastructure. Co-founder Yi He posted on X that withdrawal services were expected to resume by Sunday.
Binance's SAFU emergency reserve — a $1.2 billion fund established in 2018 as a last-resort buffer — covers roughly a third of the losses left unfrozen after industry freezes. The remainder comes from Binance's own balance sheet, which holds approximately $144 billion in assets under custody.
Markets Reel and a Record Is Broken
Bitcoin fell more than 4 percent to approximately $77,994 in the hours after the news broke, reversing a nine-percent rally that had taken place earlier in the week.
The scale is almost without precedent. Chainalysis and TRM Labs estimate that approximately $2.7 billion in cryptocurrency was stolen across the entire industry throughout 2025 — across more than 140 separate incidents. This single attack nearly doubled that annual figure in less than half an hour. The previous record holder — the Bybit breach of February 2025 — clocked in at approximately $1.5 billion, less than a quarter of what was taken from Binance on Thursday.
"It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business. For a sector that has spent years building credibility with both retail and institutional investors, the implications reach well beyond any single balance sheet. As cybersecurity expert Michael Redbord noted: at this scale, the breach is "a global security issue, not just a crypto theft."

sources.news_title: Binance Cryptocurrency exchange cyber attack: North Korean-linked Lazarus Group suspected in $6.3 billion heist
Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist
sources.text:
Hackers stole about US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest digital asset exchange, in the biggest theft in the sector’s history, which the US Secret Service is investigating with other agencies. Blockchain analytics firms point to a hacking group linked to North Korea, though there has been no official attribution.
Most of the theft took place in about 20 minutes from 20:05 GMT on Thursday, from the wallets Binance uses to process transactions, according to TRM Labs. Its chief policy officer, Ari Redbord, told the BBC that such speed “is the product of long preparation”: the attackers had funded an operator wallet 36 hours earlier and prepared in advance the signatures to authorise the transfers. According to TRM, they compromised the platform’s “signing infrastructure”.
Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said the attack “was not carried out by one person”. The initial investigation pointed to an engineer’s laptop, but “additional points of breach” were later uncovered. The attackers exploited an Ethereum network mechanism known as EIP-7702 to gain control of a wallet without passing through normal approval controls, and used a “self-destruct mechanism” to erase their traces, according to Teng, who said customer losses would be covered by the company’s protection fund, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve, and its own resources. Binance says it has begun recovering some funds. Withdrawals remain suspended and the company expects to resume them within about 40 hours; it will publish a full proof-of-reserves report on Monday.
The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds, in coordination with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident”.
About half of the stolen assets were stablecoins that their issuers — Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture — have frozen. TRM estimates that about US$2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether is beyond reach, as no company can block them.
TRM Labs and Chainalysis said they had “high confidence” that the culprit is TraderTraitor, also known as Lazarus, a North Korea-linked group the FBI blamed for the theft of about US$1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange in 2025, until now the sector’s largest. Chainalysis detected Binance funds commingling with those from another recent attack attributed to North Korean actors. Pyongyang routinely denies involvement in such thefts. Bitcoin fell about 4% after news of the attack.

Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea in what is possibly the largest financial heist of all time.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets.
Binance said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier today it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours.
It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company’s total user assets and public reserves.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.”
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called “hot” wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
“Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust,” Teng wrote.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
“This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analysts Elliptic said.
The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to U.S. blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to U.S. and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, which makes this a national security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM, said.
Binance is working with the FBI and the U.S. Secret Service, a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.
The FBI said it was “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”
The Secret Service said in a statement that its investigators “are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday.”
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it was “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”. Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance last year.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised. Bitcoin last stood at $77,355 and ether at $2,229. Binance’s BNB token was down 6.74% over the past 24 hours at $698.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher U.S. interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin’s most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expected Binance to “deliver” on ensuring no customers suffered losses. “Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security, and emerge stronger and more resilient,” he wrote today.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.

Researchers say the hack is the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, raising concerns about North Korea’s ability to finance its government and weapons programs.
The FBI is working with government and industry partners after hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, an attack researchers have linked to North Korea.
“The FBI is aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts and coordinate appropriate investigative steps,” the bureau told Nextgov/FCW. It did not attribute the intrusions to North Korea.
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs estimated that hackers transferred $6.36 billion out of Binance’s digital wallets Thursday, most of it in about 20 minutes. The company described it as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, more than four times the $1.5 billion taken from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025.
TRM attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the North Korean hackers the bureau previously blamed for the Bybit theft.
Binance allows customers to buy, sell and hold digital currencies. The attack targeted wallets the company uses to handle those assets across multiple cryptocurrency networks. The company said its preliminary investigation suggests the breach began with a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer who works on its software and operations. The attacker then accessed an internal service and submitted withdrawals without authorization.
Earlier this year, the U.S. intelligence community assessed that Pyongyang has been able to net at least $1 billion annually in cryptocurrency heists and other financial crimes to fund its weapons programs.
“Decades of investment in cybersecurity have strengthened traditional defenses, yet the growing complexity of digital banking and AI have created new vulnerabilities,” said Phoebe Hodgson, a banking and payments senior analyst at GlobalData.
Binance said it temporarily halted deposits and withdrawals while conducting security checks. It pledged to cover all losses using its emergency protection fund and company money and said it would publish an updated accounting of the assets backing customer balances once repairs were complete.
Hackers can make stolen cryptocurrency harder to recover by exchanging it for other digital currencies and moving it between wallets. After the Bybit hack, the FBI said attackers had spread the stolen funds across thousands of wallets, and the bureau urged cryptocurrency companies to block further transfers.
North Korea has been stealing cryptocurrency for years as part of a broader effort to evade sanctions and raise money for the regime and weapons research.
Its operations have also involved the use of false identities meant to obtain remote technology jobs. Earlier this month, U.S. authorities announced the disruption of “laptop farms” in Texas that helped DPRK operatives pose as U.S.-based employees and send their earnings back to the regime.

sources.text:
Cryptocurrency platform Binance yesterday said it was working to resolve a “complex attack” that affected about US$6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
The company — the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes — said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach,” contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.
Photo: Reuters
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said that it had “high confidence” the attack was orchestrated by a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group — which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Binance confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around US$6.3 billion.”
That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: US$1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.
That heist was attributed at the time to TraderTraitor.
Binance said the US$6.3 billion figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”
About US$3 billion in affected assets had been frozen, it said.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe,” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”
At about 9am GMT yesterday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended.”
“Deposits remain unaffected,” it said.
The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorized party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
However, it later said that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.”
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether — a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT — said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than US$800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.

sources.news_title: Hackers Just Committed Largest Crypto Heist In History As Cybersecurity Fears Reach Fever Pitch
sources.text:
North Korean hackers allegedly stole approximately $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance on Thursday in a record-breaking cyberattack that exposed vulnerabilities in the digital asset industry amid growing concerns over artificial intelligence-powered cybercrime.
The attack drained billions of dollars from Binance-controlled wallets in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, which attributed the breach to North Korea’s state-sponsored TraderTraitor hacking unit. The massive theft unfolded as cybersecurity researchers warned that North Korean operatives were increasingly using AI to impersonate employees, develop malicious software and conduct sophisticated cyberattacks against financial institutions and cryptocurrency companies. (RELATED: Top Trump Dinner Bidders Stash Cash On Exchanges That Shut Out Americans)
“Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the company said in an official statement Friday.
The company said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were compromised, although its investigation uncovered additional potential points of intrusion.
TRM Labs reported that approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency moved from Binance wallets across ten blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Tron.
The firm said the attack appeared to involve compromised infrastructure responsible for authorizing cryptocurrency transactions, allowing the perpetrators to initiate unauthorized transfers across multiple blockchain networks.
Investigators also identified evidence that preparations began at least 36 hours before the theft, including transactions used to test the malicious code eventually deployed against Binance wallets.
TRM Labs attributed the operation to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group previously linked to the $1.5 billion cryptocurrency theft from Bybit in February 2025.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the Bybit attack to North Korea, identifying TraderTraitor as responsible for stealing the digital assets.
The Binance theft was approximately four times larger than the Bybit attack, which previously ranked among the largest cryptocurrency heists on record.
Binance announced Friday that it worked with industry partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in affected assets, leaving billions more beyond its immediate control.
The company pledged to cover customer losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users, an emergency reserve intended to protect customers, alongside additional corporate resources.
Binance said deposits were operating normally, although withdrawals remained temporarily suspended while security teams investigated the incident. The exchange expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours.
Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle were among the companies that helped freeze stolen assets, according to TRM Labs.
Investigators found that the perpetrators attempted to exchange stolen stablecoins for other cryptocurrencies before issuers could intervene, illustrating the challenges of recovering assets once they move beyond centralized financial controls.
The theft rattled cryptocurrency markets Friday, with Bitcoin falling to a six-week low and Ether declining to a two-month low, according to Reuters.
The Binance attack followed a separate security breach Thursday involving Polymarket, a prediction market platform that temporarily suspended international trading after a third-party provider was compromised.
Blockchain intelligence firm Bitquery identified approximately $2.73 million in unauthorized withdrawals affecting 737 accounts over roughly one hour.
Polymarket said it identified and resolved the vulnerability, referred the incident to law enforcement and would reimburse affected users. Trading subsequently resumed.
Investigators have not established a connection between the Binance and Polymarket attacks.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence warned Thursday that North Korean cybercriminal groups were increasingly incorporating AI into their operations, using the technology to research potential victims, generate convincing fraudulent identities and scale phishing campaigns.
The report identified North Korean hackers using AI to produce fabricated job applications, manipulate images and videos, impersonate recruiters and develop malicious content designed to deceive potential targets.
Microsoft assessed that AI adoption among North Korean hacking groups was widespread, although the operations remained directed by humans rather than fully autonomous systems.
The findings highlighted a growing cybersecurity concern: AI can make established hacking techniques faster, more convincing and more difficult for security teams to detect.
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported in September that North Korean cybercriminal operations were increasingly incorporating AI into cryptocurrency theft campaigns, including social engineering, software supply chain manipulation and automated backdoor development.
The researchers found that cybercriminals were moving beyond using AI to generate messages and increasingly employing automated tools to accelerate stages of an attack.
Google previously documented a North Korean-linked operation targeting a financial technology company through a compromised Telegram account, a fraudulent Zoom meeting and reportedly AI-generated video intended to deceive the victim.
Investigators have not publicly established that AI played a role in Thursday’s Binance attack, but the incident illustrated the potential financial consequences of security failures at major digital asset platforms.
Google’s September threat intelligence report also warned that AI-assisted cyberattacks could reduce the amount of time defenders have to detect and stop intrusions, identifying an operation in which attackers compromised a cloud resource and launched an AI-assisted credential harvesting campaign in less than six hours.

sources.text:
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest cryptocurrency exchange, in a significant digital theft. The theft occurred by draining cryptocurrencies from wallets used for transactions, according to Binance and blockchain analysis. Initially, Binance believed a compromised laptop was responsible for the attack, but further investigation revealed more points of breach. The exchange has a secure asset fund, worth $1 billion in Bitcoin, set up to protect users in case of security issues. Co-CEO Richard Teng announced that the losses would be covered by this fund and the company’s resources.
The attack compromised Binance’s signing infrastructure, which is responsible for authorizing transactions. This allowed the attackers to give instructions that emptied the wallets. The breach happened quickly, within about 20 minutes, shortly after 2000 GMT on a Thursday. Once the funds were stolen, attackers tried to quickly move them to avoid detection. Some cryptocurrencies can be frozen by their issuers, which has led to half of the stolen assets being frozen.
Analysis suggests that the attack may be linked to North Korean hackers, with similarities to previous incidents. Binance has not identified the attackers, and North Korea typically denies such allegations. Fund movements have shown links to other recent attacks attributed to North Korean groups, indicating a possible connection.
Approximately half of the stolen assets were stablecoins, which have been frozen, limiting the attackers’ options to convert them into cash. However, some of the stolen Bitcoin and Ether remain untraceable because these currencies cannot be frozen by any central authority. The attackers might attempt to launder the stolen coins but will face challenges as time passes, which could lead to them being blacklisted by exchanges.
