sources.news_title: World’s largest crypto exchange hit by suspected North Korean hack in world’s largest heist - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
(CNN) — Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended withdrawals after hackers broke into its digital wallets and stole $6 billion in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever.
The exchange said Friday that it has begun recovering affected assets and was continuing to work with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace additional funds.
An initial investigation suggested the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” Binance said late on Thursday. Blockchain evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea, according to multiple crypto-tracing firms.
A team of cryptocurrency firms managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money.
Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said on X that the attack was not a “one-click” action, but rather a complex process. The investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual nor found evidence of any wallet private key leak.
Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds. The crypto exchange expects withdrawal services to resume by Sunday morning.
Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” pointing out that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist.
“Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons.
“I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds.
Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including bitcoin and ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack.
CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. Pyongyang has previously denied hacking allegations.
In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money.
The FBI said in a statement Friday that it is “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”
A spokesperson for the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime, said the agency’s “investigators are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle [the company behind the US dollar-backed stablecoin USDC], to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday. We are also coordinating closely with the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and law enforcement partners to identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice.”
If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes.
North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms.
A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim.
Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry.
Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch.
However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. He was sentenced to four months in federal prison, and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in October last year.
Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange, pushing back against any suggestion to the contrary in a spat on X with Elon Musk.

Cybersecurity breaches are increasingly escalating, thanks to AI powering both defenders and attackers. North Korean hackers are suspected in the theft of $6.3 billion from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange in what reportedly is the “largest bank heist in human history.”

TraderTraitor, the North Korean hacking group suspected of pulling off the heist, is known for unparalleled lootings by using algorithms to spread the riches across global crypto networks faster than any human could – making them virtually impossible to recover.

“The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism … making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate,” Teng said, adding that Binance’s security team is still deep in the throes of the investigation.
Binance said Friday it has started to recover some of the stolen assets. About $2.8 billion was quickly frozen by stablecoin providers – but roughly $3 billion is likely gone forever, as it was unable to be frozen, according to analytics firms.

sources.news_title: The Largest Heist in History: Hackers Steal $6 Billion in Crypto from Binance
sources.text:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended withdrawals after hackers stole $6 billion from its digital wallets in what is being described as the biggest financial heist on record.
Axios reports that Binance co-founder Yi He announced on X that the exchange had suspended deposits and withdrawals following the suspected breach. “User funds are safe,” she wrote, adding, “Binance will cover all hacking losses.” Multiple reports put the amount stolen from the exchange at $6 billion in cryptocurrency.
Co-CEO Richard Teng also commented on the issue, saying, “Bottom Line — your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.”
Binance published an official disclosure of the incident in a post on X. According to the exchange, “Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
On wallet security, Binance was blunt: “We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”
As for the money, the company wrote, “The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B. We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.” That leaves roughly half the estimated total still out there.
Binance also moved to reassure customers they won’t be the ones footing the bill. “Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company’s funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete,” the company said.
The exchange listed three immediate steps it took in response: “As an immediate precaution, Binance has: temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorisation; engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.”
It also promised more detail later. “We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified,” the company said, adding, “Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The breach lands in the middle of what’s being called “Black October,” a stretch marked by a wave of cyberattacks, data breaches and bugs surfaced by AI tools. It also echoes last year’s theft at the Bybit exchange, where North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion in crypto. North Korea has built hacking and scamming into an industrial-scale operation, running crypto heists alongside a scheme that tricks Western companies into unknowingly hiring North Korean workers.
A team of cryptocurrency firms has already frozen about $3 billion of the stolen funds, even as the rest keeps moving. Chainalysis, one of the firms tracking the money, said it was watching funds shift “across multiple blockchains,” including bitcoin and ethereum. A spokesperson for the firm told CNN it had “high confidence” that North Korea was behind the hack.
Two other tracing firms reached the same conclusion. TRM Labs attributed the theft to an elite North Korean hacking unit, saying the assessment was “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence” and noting that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence agreed. An analyst there told CNN the firm’s conclusion came from “analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents.” The same analyst warned that getting the rest of the money back won’t happen fast: “I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet.”
Read more at Axios here.

sources.news_title: How the record-breaking $6.3 billion heist in crypto history unfolded
sources.text:
France24
                
30 Oct 2026, 19:22 GMT+10
            
Hackersstole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggestcryptocurrencyexchange, in a record digital asset theft.
Here's what we know so far:
About $6.3 billion of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records.
Read moreBinance hit by $6.3 billion security breach in potential record crypto heist
Binance said in astatement on Xthat it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop. "However, our subsequentinvestigationhas uncovered additional points of breach," it added, without elaborating.
The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.
Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources.
According to US blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorizes transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 2000 GMT on Thursday.
Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets.
An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely.
"In layman's terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money," said Joshua Chu, aHong Konglawyer who works on crypto cases.
Several US blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers.
Teng said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers, whileNorth Korearoutinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea's mission in Geneva and embassy inChinadid not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year's attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which theFBIattributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft.
Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.
About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, theTrumpfamily's crypto venture.
That doesn't mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers' ability to convert them into cash.
TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about $2.4 billion worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach.
"No company issues bitcoin or ether and no company can freeze either one," said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm inSingapore.
"The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys."
Market participants said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds.
"The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers they essentially get blacklisted," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company.
"In reality a lot of the proceeds of hacks ... (can only be laundered) in the first few hours, but after that happens, you have a lot of different players who know those are marked funds ... and they usually sit there for years."
The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole $2.9 billion of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs.
The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

sources.news_title: Crypto industry suffers 'largest bank heist in human history' as billions stolen in Binance hack
sources.text:
Cryptocurrency worth more than $6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) has been drained from one of the world’s largest digital asset exchanges in what industry observers are calling the biggest bank heist in human history. According to a report from Sky News, the security breach struck Binance, a dominant platform for trading digital assets, which said it was urgently establishing the full facts of the attack.
Deposits and withdrawals were suspended for customers as the company insisted that user funds remained safe and that all losses from the hacking would be covered.
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit, and said the entire operation was completed in just 20 minutes. That timeline would make it the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, surpassing the $1.5 billion stolen from the Bybit exchange last year.
Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said the company’s “initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop.” In a post on X, he clarified the scale of the intrusion: “To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action.
It involved a more complex attack process.” The firm stated that its investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual and that teams were working closely with law enforcement.
Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, described the incident on X as looking like a hack. Ari Redbord, chief policy officer at TRM Labs, told Sky News: “This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response… Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale.”
He noted that the attackers moved billions of dollars across eight blockchain networks in roughly 15 minutes. The same group has been linked by the FBI to the earlier Bybit breach, and investigators believe the perpetrators spent at least 36 hours preparing for the strike.
“The theft shows how exposed the system is to sophisticated attackers moving at a speed we have never seen,” Redbord added. After the breach was identified, more than $3 billion (£2.2 billion) in digital assets were frozen, potentially limiting the attackers’ ability to cash out. Even so, the remaining holdings under their control were estimated at about $2.4 billion (£1.8 billion) in Bitcoin and Ether, the two largest cryptocurrencies by market value.
Izabella Kaminska, editor of the independent publication The Blind Spot, which covers the crypto industry, told Sky News the episode “appears to be a highly sophisticated and well-rehearsed attack.” The breach arrives amid rising concern that major cyber vulnerabilities across the financial system could soon be exposed or exploited by AI agents.
While the crypto sector has long marketed itself as decentralized and resistant to censorship, Kaminska observed that the vast majority of platforms—and in some cases the assets themselves—remain structurally centralized in ways that mirror conventional banking.

sources.news_title: North Korean Hackers Steal Over $6 Billion From Crypto Exchange In Biggest Heist In Human History
sources.text:
There are a number of factors that have drawn people to cryptocurrencies, including a system that’s designed to make it virtually impossible for people to steal what’s yours. However, hackers in North Korea figured out how to infiltrate the world’s biggest exchange while claiming what is believed to be the largest heist ever staged.
It’s been more than 15 years since a mysterious figure known as “Satoshi Nakamoto” penned a paper outlining the vision for what became Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency that was mined for the first time in 2009.
What initially seemed like a bit of a fad primarily reserved for a niche community of technologically savvy futurists eventually burst into the mainstream as Bitcoin and other forms of crypto experienced a massive boom toward the start of the 2020s, and as things currently stand, the entire cryptocurrency industry boasts a $2.6 trillion market cap.
There are a number of platforms you can turn to in order to manage your assets, and none of them do more business than Binance, the exchange that lists more than 900 different coins and handles close to $15 billion worth of transactions each day.
However, it’s been targeted by hackers who made off with a truly massive score.
North Korean hackers made history after stealing more than $6 billion from Binance
Most people initially stored crypto on a physical hard drive known as a wallet, and the only way to access the asset was through a lenghty private key that was impossible to randomly guess to the point where some people who’ve misplaced theirs have spent years attempting to recover a potentially lost fortune.
However, digital wallets that are stored online have become an increasingly popular option, but they are inherently more susceptible to being targeted by cybercriminals on the hunt for a potentially massive payday.
According to The New York Times, the potential downsides of going that route have been firmly highlighted by an incident involving Binance, which was founded in China in 2017 en route to becoming the biggest exchange in the crypto space.
On Thursday, the company confirmed it had been infiltrated in an operation that’s been linked back to “North Korea’s elite hacking unit,” which staged what was described as a “complex hack” involving multiple “points of breach.”
The group stole digital assets that were initially valued at $6.3 billion, making it the largest-ever crypto heist and seemingly the biggest single theft of tangible currency in history (a $1.5 billion hack of Bybit in 2025, which was also traced back to North Korea, previously topped that list).
Binance users do not have the privilege of having their holdings covered by the FDIC or similar agencies. However, the company has pledged to cover all the losses after temporarily freezing withdrawals and deposits and hopes to resume business as normal within the next couple of days.

'Biggest hack in history'
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
"Your money is safe and we're covering every loss," Teng said on X. "Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual." 
"It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said as crypto prices fell broadly.
Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised.
BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to CoinGecko, while shaky confidence hit listed crypto exchange shares.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global, which said it was unaffected, slid 4.8%, while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
Compromised laptop
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
"Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said. Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach.
Mark Karpeles, former chief of defunct Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox, which collapsed a dozen years ago after $500 million in bitcoin was stolen, said attackers probably accessed private keys for at least two Binance wallets.
"Binance appears to have split its assets across multiple systems, ensuring a hack can only affect a part of the assets, but even so a single hack is a large loss," he said.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Hack size tops Binance secure asset fund
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
World Liberty Financial said it worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
In September, Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.
"The broader credit and industry implications will depend on the ultimate losses, affected counterparties, asset recovery, and importantly, whether the incident leads to wider disruption or loss of confidence across the digital-asset ecosystem," said Cristiano Ventricelli, vice president, digital assets at Moody’s Ratings.

sources.news_title: Binance $6.3B Hack: Firms Blame North Korea
sources.text:
Two blockchain intelligence firms say North Korea’s elite hacking unit stole about $6.36 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, which would make it the largest crypto theft on record. No government has publicly confirmed the attribution, and Binance has not confirmed it either.
What is established
TRM, a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm, said an attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes. TRM posted its findings on Thursday, and the Associated Press reported them on Friday, October 30, 2026. The AP rounded the loss to “more than $6 billion.”
Binance says it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. The exchange says customer deposits were unaffected, withdrawals are suspended and should resume within a day or two, and it will cover all losses.
Who is blamed, and on what evidence
TRM attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit, and said it made that judgment “with high confidence.” The evidence it cited is a pattern: “Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack.”
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and chief executive of the firm Chainalysis, wrote on X that the theft was “likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor.” DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s formal name. The AP’s account gives no further evidence from Chainalysis.
The Bybit comparison is worth separating from this case. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the February 2025 theft of $1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange. That was a government finding about a different theft. For Binance, the AP reports no FBI or other government attribution. A match with earlier heists is a reason for suspicion, and “high confidence” is a private firm’s judgment, not a legal finding.
What Binance has said, and how its account has shifted
A Binance spokesperson, asked about the North Korea link, said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
On X, Binance first said its initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop. A later investigation, it said, uncovered additional “points of breach.” Binance also said it found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, and that it will release more technical details when its investigation is complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder, who stepped down as chief executive in 2023 and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2025, posted on X: “User funds are safe!” He said the theft “does look like a hack on Binance” and that, as a shareholder, he expects all user funds to be fully covered.
A competing theory, flagged as speculation
Kok Tin Gan, chief executive of the security firm NyxLab, offered a different reading. “This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said. That is his speculation, not a confirmed finding, and it sits uneasily with Binance’s statement that it found no private key leak. Which account is right is not yet known.
What is not yet confirmed
The AP report does not give a calendar date for the theft. It does not establish how the attacker got in, how much of the remainder beyond the roughly $3 billion frozen can be recovered, or whether any government will formally name North Korea. Binance’s promise to resume withdrawals within a day or two is also a statement of intent, not a completed fact.
Why it matters
If a government confirms the attribution, this would be the second large exchange theft pinned on TraderTraitor, after Bybit. It would also raise a practical question for U.S. officials about whether exchange security standards have kept pace with a state-backed adversary that has now been tied to two of the biggest thefts in the industry’s history. For now, that is a conditional: the proof so far is a firm’s pattern analysis and Binance’s own incomplete account.
Sources
- Associated Press, via The Philadelphia Inquirer: “Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance” (October 30, 2026)
- Statements from TRM, Chainalysis, Binance, Changpeng Zhao and NyxLab are as quoted by the Associated Press. Right Side News did not independently review the original TRM post.
- Featured image: Flag of North Korea (public domain flag design), from the Right Side News media library.
How this article was made: Right Side News researched and drafted this article with the help of AI tools. Sources are linked so readers can check them. Spot an error? Tell us in the comments and we will correct it.

sources.news_title: Binance hit by 'largest crypto theft on record' as North Korean hackers steal $6.3bn in just 20 minutes
sources.text:
Binance hit by 'largest crypto theft on record' as North Korean hackers steal $6.3bn in just 20 minutes
Lazarus is breaking its own records year after year
- Attackers allegedly stole $6.36 billion from Binance in a record-breaking cryptocurrency exchange breach
- Investigators linked the attack to North Korea’s Lazarus Group, exploiting access from a compromised engineer
- Binance said customer funds remain safe, while authorities and partners froze billions in stolen assets
Cybercriminals, allegedly from an infamous North Korean hacking organization, have gained access to one of the biggest cryptocurrency exchanges on the planet - Binance - and in less than half an hour withdrew $6.36 billion worth of different tokens.
Security researchers TRM Labs said the attack was carried out by a group called TraderTraitor, which it describes as “North Korea’s premier hacking unit”.
“We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources,” TRM Labs said in a report, noting that TraderTraitor is part of Lazarus Group, North Korea’s state-sponsored threat actor blamed for some of the biggest crypto heists in history, with the FBI blaming it for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack that took place on February 21, 2025.
Gone in 20 minutes
Binance’s experts, as well as independent researchers, are still piecing together what happened, so information might change throughout the day(s). What we know so far is that a DevOps engineer had their laptop compromised, which was confirmed by Richard Teng, Binance co-CEO, in a LinkedIn post.
“That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” he said.
Right now, no one really knows what exactly happened and what it means that a DevOps engineer’s laptop was compromised. However, we do know that Lazarus is famous for running operations DreamJob and Contagious Interview, in which they set up fake companies and fake jobs, and then approach software engineers working on crypto projects. They entice them with lucrative job offers and exciting opportunities, and sneak malware during the multiple interview rounds.
But Binance’s security measures are more robust than that, and simply installing malware on one device could not have sufficed. Teng confirmed that, too, saying “the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single "one-click" action. It involved a more complex attack process.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Funds are SAFU
TRM Labs said the attackers pulled funds from 10 different chains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Tron, Solana, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, and Polygon. The Ethereum chain was the hardest one hit, losing roughly $3.79 billion. It could be because of the chain’s smart contracts feature, which allowed the attackers to keep withdrawing funds as they were landing into the wallet.
Binance is one of the biggest and most popular cryptocurrency exchanges on planet Earth, and as such it holds billions of dollars in user funds. This attack, however, did not target user funds, but rather Binance itself. This was confirmed by both Teng and TRM Labs, with the co-CEO saying “your funds are safe”, and “Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds.”
In response to the attack, Binance temporarily restricted deposits and withdrawals. Numerous users took to X this morning to say their transaction requests were denied. The police and other relevant entities were notified, and around $3 billion were already frozen on-chain, apparently.
Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, TRM Labs confirmed, while Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly $2.7 billion.
What’s particularly interesting about this incident is how the market responded. In 2013, when Mt.Gox (at the time the biggest crypto exchange in the world) got hacked for $450 million, it was considered a “black swan” event, sending bitcoin down by more than a third (35%) in a few weeks. The 2025 Bybit hack sent BTC down approximately 7.5%. In response to the Binance hack, BTC dropped a measly 6.7%, which is just another Friday in the crypto world.
Phishing incoming
Trouble always comes in pairs, and this Binance hack will most likely be no exception. Security researchers NordVPN are warning users that other hacking groups might try to take advantage of the news to target users with phishing emails.
“Another risk is criminals exploiting the confusion and fear among crypto owners on other platforms. An email claiming your funds are at risk, a fake support account offering help or a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a ‘safe wallet’ could be an attempt to steal from you,” said Marijus Briedis, Chief Technology Officer at NordVPN.
“Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust. Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase. Pressure to act immediately should be a reason to pause and verify the request.”
“These steps can reduce the risk of someone taking over your account, but they cannot prevent a breach of the platform itself. Cryptocurrency firms typically have watertight cybersecurity, as they are digital-first businesses, so if one can be involved in the biggest hack in history, it shows just how lucrative a single flaw can be.”

sources.news_title: Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded
sources.text:
Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded
About $6.3bn of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records.
Binance said in a statement on X that it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop. "However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," it added, without elaborating.
The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.
Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources.
According to US blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorises transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 8pm on Thursday.
Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets.
An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely.
"In layman's terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money," said Joshua Chu, a Hong Kong lawyer who works on crypto cases.
Several US blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers.
Teng said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers, while North Korea routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea's mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year's attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft.
Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.
About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture.
That doesn't mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers' ability to convert them into cash.
TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about $2.4bn worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach.
"No company issues bitcoin or ether and no company can freeze either one," said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm in Singapore.
"The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys."
Market participants said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser-known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds.
"The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers — they essentially get blacklisted," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company.
"In reality, a lot of the proceeds of hacks ... (can only be laundered) in the first few hours, but after that happens, you have a lot of different players who know those are marked funds ... and they usually sit there for years."
The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole $2.9bn of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs.
The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.
Reuters

sources.news_title: Binance hackers stole $6.3 billion in record-breaking crypto heist
sources.text:
Binance has disclosed that $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what’s believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record. In a series of updates posted to X, the crypto exchange said that user funds are safe, and that around $3 billion of the impacted assets have been frozen so far.
Binance hackers stole $6.3 billion in record-breaking crypto heist
$3 billion of stolen assets have been frozen so far, and Binance has promised to ‘cover all losses.’
Binance has publicly committed to covering any losses resulting from the hack. The company has an emergency reserve fund of around $1.3 billion (at last valuation) to protect user assets in these situations, and said it has also reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident — $5 billion of which is “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” Binance reported on X. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
The company shared details about the compromised laptop that belongs to one of its DevOps engineers in a prior update, saying it allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Deposits and withdrawals have been suspended in response to the hack, and the affected address has had its authorization revoked.
“To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action. It involved a more complex attack process,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”
Binance may not be pointing fingers at who’s behind the attack, but blockchain analysis firms TRM and Chainalysis both attribute it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime hacking group that has a history of stealing funds from cryptocurrency exchanges. This is the largest known cryptocurrency heist in history — four times higher than the previous record, when $1.46 billion was stolen from Bybit last year — and according to TRM, most of the theft occurred over a period of just 20 minutes.
This isn’t the first time Binance has been hacked, having suffered a previous security breach in 2019 in which $40 million worth of crypto assets (valued at the time) were stolen. The latest hack comes as cases of large-scale crypto theft are escalating, however, after several heists were disclosed by crypto companies in September. There are also new concerns around how AI tools can be used maliciously against the industry, with OpenAI reporting earlier this month that one of its models managed to swipe fake crypto on an Ethereum test network it didn’t have access to.
“This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response... Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale,” TRM chief policy officer Ari Redbord said in a statement to Sky News. “The theft shows how exposed the system is to sophisticated attackers moving at a speed we have never seen.”

sources.news_title: Massive $6 billion Binance crypto hack likely has small impact in the Netherlands
sources.text:
Massive $6 billion Binance crypto hack likely has small impact in the Netherlands
Cryptocurrency platform Binance has reported that $6.3 billion (5.6 billion euros) is linked to what is being called the biggest hack ever recorded in the cryptocurrency industry. Roughly half of the funds have been frozen in an effort to stop hackers from carrying out large-scale theft at the world's largest crypto exchange. Binance used to have a significant presence in the Netherlands but exited the market a few years ago when it failed to reach a deal with De Nederlandsche Bank.
"The estimated total impact amounts to approximately $6.3 billion," Binance wrote in a post on X. "We are working with blockchain partners to freeze the affected funds. So far, approximately $3 billion has been frozen on-chain."
The hack at Binance is unlikely to have a significant impact on Dutch cryptocurrency investors, according to Mauro Halve, chairman of the Dutch Association of Crypto Service Providers (NVC). The organization represents regulated crypto companies in the Netherlands. "Trading on Binance has been prohibited for some time, so we consider it very unlikely that Dutch investors will be affected."
The exchange has temporarily halted all withdrawals, but expects the service to be restored within 48 hours. Binance also assured customers that their funds remain "safe" and that it will reimburse any losses resulting from the incident.
Binance revealed overnight that it had suffered a "security incident." In response, the exchange announced several measures, including freezing billions of dollars in cryptocurrency and temporarily halting trading in some products.
Binance suspects the security breach may have originated from a software developer's laptop that had been “compromised.” Blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs, meanwhile, has attributed the theft to hackers from North Korea.
The Financial Times reported earlier this month that the European Union had raised questions about Binance continuing to operate within the bloc. The cryptocurrency exchange had failed to secure a license earlier this year and was subsequently required to wind down some of its EU operations.
Binance withdrew from the Dutch market in 2023 after being fined millions of euros by the Dutch central bank a year earlier. DNB imposed the penalty because the exchange had provided cryptocurrency services in the Netherlands without obtaining the required registration.
The news initially triggered a sell-off in the cryptocurrency market, with Bitcoin falling by almost 5 percent and Ethereum dropping nearly 6 percent. Both have since recovered most of their losses.
DNB said in 2022, when it fined Binance millions of euros, that the exchange had "a very large number of customers" in the Netherlands. Halve noted that investors often use several cryptocurrency platforms simultaneously, unlike traditional bank accounts. "Binance was one of the most popular crypto platforms in the Netherlands for a long time," he said.
"Consumers should check whether the cryptocurrency service provider they intend to use has a license and where it is licensed," the Netherlands Authority for the Financial Markets (AFM) said. Europe has introduced MiCAR, a set of rules governing cryptocurrencies and crypto services. "If service providers do not have a license in Europe, customers should be aware that they are not subject to MiCAR supervision and that this carries additional risks."
Bloomberg described the Binance incident as the largest cryptocurrency hack in history. The previous record was set in February 2025, when hackers stole $1.5 billion from crypto exchange Bybit. The FBI later attributed that attack to North Korean hackers, Bloomberg reported.
Reporting by ANP

sources.news_title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
sources.text:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.
Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.
Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”
The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.
“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.
The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.
Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.
Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.
Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.
“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”
“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”
TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.
“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”
While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”
Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

The cryptocurrency platform pledged to cover all losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.
The company said preliminary investigations suggested that the incident may have involved a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which allegedly enabled an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

sources.text:
Binance, world’s largest crypto exchange, investigates potential $6.3B hack
LOS ANGELES - Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it was investigating a potential security breach after its founder said the incident "does look like a hack." The company later estimated the total impact at more than $6 billion, potentially making it one of the largest cryptocurrency security incidents on record.
It wasn’t immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.
What they're saying:
"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.
"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.
RELATED: DOJ: Elder fraud cases tied to nearly $4.8B in losses, 711,000 victims
The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.
"Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.
What's next:
Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."
"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.
Why you should care:
Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.
The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.
RELATED: Dollar General sued by FTC and 20 states, accused of overcharging customers
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The backstory:
Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family’s crypto enterprises.

The information came from statements and posts published by Binance, including its estimate of the potential $6.3 billion impact, the temporary suspension of deposits and withdrawals, and its claim that user funds were safe. sources.news_title: World’s biggest crypto exchange hit by record $6.3 billion hack
sources.text:
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record hack, putting hundreds of millions of people’s money at risk.
Binance said on Friday that suspected hackers had taken around $6.3 billion, which could make it the biggest ever crypto heist. A blockchain analysis firm blamed North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group for the breach—as Binance suspended withdrawals with the value of cryptocurrencies plummeting.
Kathryn Westmore, the director of financial crime at UK Finance, told Newsweek: “TraderTraitors [is] believed to be a state-sponsored North Korean hacking group who have carried out other hacks on other platforms, although not at the scale of the Binance hack.”
Read More on News
She said that although the hackers attacked Binance, users’ own security on their personal devices would have played a part in whether their wallets were targeted.
Westmore said: “It can be as complex an attack as you like, but it ultimately depends on a person’s device becoming compromised, whether with malware or something else.
“The human element is so interesting. So many hacks or cyber attacks start with a person doing it or doing something which ends up infecting their device and the network.”
Responding to today’s attack, Binance said its initial investigations of the “security incident” indicated that the laptop of a software engineer at the company may have been compromised, which allowed hackers into the platform’s systems and ultimately to green-light withdrawals.
Binance was hit with a crypto heist in 2022, when a hacker artificially created 2 million BNB tokens, amounting to around $570 million.
Although the platform stepped in, the attacker was still able to take around $115 million.
After this latest huge hack, Blockchain company TRM Labs said it had “high confidence” North Korean hackers were behind the attack.
It said: “TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit. We make this judgment with high confidence.”
The group added: “We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources. The FBI named the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst.
“The laundering observed so far, built on large swaps through market makers and lending protocols, differs from the bridge-heavy pattern that followed Bybit.”
Meanwhile, intelligence analyst James Seyffart told Bloomberg: “Hot wallets [digital wallets connected to a live network] getting drained is not something new to crypto, but the amount would be a meaningful hack on the largest crypto exchange. It’s definitely a bad look. And this is one after another.”
BNB, formerly known as Binance Coin, dropped by more than 4.7 percent. Bitcoin fell approximately 4.5 percent to $76,368 before recovering to $78,434.
How the Heist Went Down
TRM believes the attack took around 36 hours to prepare, when the main operator got “three small withdrawals from Tornado Cash, a service that obscures where crypto comes from, starting the morning of October 28.”
Then the hacker started the attack, using code to attack two wallets. The group tested the code on a third wallet before funnelling the money used back to their accounts.
Four hours later, the hack began.
In the space of just four minutes between 8:05 p.m. and 8:09 p.m., five Binance hot wallets sent 233.46 million of the cryptocurrency XRP to one of the hackers’ addresses. Each wallet was left with only its minimum balance.
One minute later, Binance wallets on Optimism and Solana were hit. At 8:20 p.m., a Binance Bitcoin hot wallet was taken over. The hackers sent themselves 18,270 BTC and split them into 1,000 BTC and 100 BTC pieces, a technique known as creating a "peel chain" that obscures the journey of funds. Finally, the attackers sent themselves 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX from a Binance hot wallet on Tron.
What Binance Users Should Do After Record $6.3 Billion Crypto Hack
Westmore told Newsweek: “It's highly likely that we're going to see a wave of fraudsters contacting potential victims and asking for payment to help them get their money back (which they can't do). Based on the statements from Binance, their money should be safe.
“However, we don't know what, if any, personal data may have been breached, so people should monitor for any signs that their personal data is being used by criminals or has been sold.”
Binance have said it will cover the costs of the massive hack.
Although he no longer runs the company, Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said on X: “I expect all user funds will be fully recovered.” He added: “It does look like a hack on Binance.”
Zhao was pardoned for money laundering charges by President Donald Trump in 2025. At the time, the president's use of executive clemency drew criticism from former U.S. Pardon Attorney Elizabeth G. Oyer and renewed questions about political influence over the Justice Department.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen over $1.56 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack,” while Circle chief Jeremy Allaire said his firm had frozen more than 800 million USDC.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Emma Lee-Sang
Update 10/30/26, 7:07 a.m. ET: This article was updated with additional information.

The exchange, which has over 335 million registered users and over $162.8 billion in assets, added: ‘User funds remain safe.’

sources.text:
Binance Hit By Record Crypto Hack. Investigators Are Pointing at North Korea.
The exchange has pledged to cover customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and company resources.
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has been hit by an estimated $6.3 billion cyberattack, potentially the largest crypto theft on record. Blockchain investigators linking the breach to North Korean hackers.
The attack involved unauthorized transfers from Binance-controlled wallets across 10 blockchain networks. Most of the stolen assets were moved within roughly 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs, which traced approximately $6.36 billion in transactions.
Binance confirmed the security breach Friday and said it had worked with blockchain partners to freeze approximately $3 billion in affected assets. The exchange pledged to cover customer losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, and company resources.
The scale of the attack exceeds the $1.5 billion stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in February 2025, previously the largest known crypto heist.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed that theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group that has targeted cryptocurrency businesses.
TRM Labs has now linked the Binance attack to the same group, citing its analysis of blockchain transactions and other intelligence. However, the company has not publicly identified the perpetrators, and the investigation remains ongoing.
The exchange initially said the breach may have involved a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, potentially allowing attackers to access a service container and initiate unauthorized withdrawals.
But subsequent investigations uncovered additional points of compromise, indicating that the attack involved a more complicated process.
In its official security update, Binance said investigators had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked. These keys are digital credentials used to authorize cryptocurrency transactions.
The company has not yet established the full sequence of events and said it would release a detailed technical report once its investigation is complete.
TRM Labs' analysis found that the attackers had prepared parts of the operation at least 36 hours before the theft, setting up computer code and testing transactions ahead of the main attack.
The stolen assets included Bitcoin, Ether and several stablecoins, which are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a fixed value, typically against the U.S. dollar.
Ethereum accounted for approximately $3.79 billion of the transfers, while Bitcoin represented another $1.47 billion. Other affected networks included Tron, Solana and the XRP Ledger.
The attackers also exploited a feature of Ethereum known as EIP-7702, which allows a wallet to authorize software that can execute transactions on its behalf.
TRM Labs found that the attackers used preauthorized transactions to gain control of a Binance wallet and transfer its holdings to addresses they controlled.
The security firm said the activity across multiple blockchains pointed to a possible compromise of Binance's transaction-signing infrastructure, although the exchange has not confirmed that explanation.
Efforts to stop the stolen funds from moving began shortly after the attack was detected. Stablecoin issuers including Tether and Circle froze large quantities of affected tokens, preventing them from being transferred or exchanged. Ripple and other blockchain organizations also participated in the response.
TRM Labs identified approximately $2.7 billion in frozen assets during its initial investigation, while Binance later confirmed a higher total of around $3 billion.
Freezing cryptocurrency prevents further movement of the affected assets but does not necessarily mean the funds have been returned to their owners.
The attackers had already converted some of the stolen stablecoins into other digital currencies before restrictions could be imposed.
TRM Labs said the perpetrators exchanged large amounts of stablecoins for Ether through decentralized trading platforms, while other funds were moved through lending services.
The firm identified more than 420,000 Ether and 18,270 Bitcoin, worth approximately $2.4 billion at the time of its analysis, in assets beyond the direct freezing powers of stablecoin issuers.
The incident also disrupted Binance's services. The company initially suspended deposits and withdrawals while conducting security checks. In a subsequent service update Friday, it said deposits were operating normally but withdrawals remained paused while it strengthened security controls.
Binance said it expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours of that update, although it had not announced a firm reopening time.
The exchange is working with law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence companies to trace the remaining assets and identify those responsible.
It also plans to publish an updated proof-of-reserves statement after completing its security work. The statement is intended to show the digital assets held by the exchange against customer balances.
Binance has not provided a final estimate of the amount it expects to recover, while investigators continue monitoring cryptocurrency held in wallets associated with the attack.

sources.news_title: North Korean hackers steal €5.85 billion from Binance
sources.text:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been struck by a cyberattack in which state-backed North Korean operatives drained roughly $6.36 billion (€5.85 billion) in digital assets across 10 distinct blockchains, according to leading blockchain analytics firms.
The heist represents the single largest theft in the history of the digital asset industry, about four times the $1.5 billion (€1.38 billion) taken from Dubai-based exchange Bybit in February 2025, according to TRM Labs.
According to forensic assessments released by TRM Labs and Chainalysis, the raid began at 8.05pm UTC (9.05pm Brussels time) on October 29. The vast majority of the capital was moved in a coordinated blitz lasting approximately 20 minutes.
Investigators attribute the breach to TraderTraitor, an elite cyber warfare unit operating under Pyongyang’s state intelligence apparatus.
TRM Labs said it made the attribution “with high confidence”, describing the group as a subunit of North Korea’s Lazarus Group. The FBI blamed the same unit for the Bybit theft.
Chainalysis chief executive Jonathan Levin said his investigators had found proceeds from the September hack of exchange Bitget mixed with funds taken from Binance.
Initial findings from Binance’s own investigation indicate the breach may have originated from the compromise of a company engineer’s laptop, subsequently granting the perpetrators access to Binance’s hot-wallet transaction signing architecture. The exchange said it had found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.
On the Ethereum network, where the single largest portion of capital was taken (roughly $3.79 billion or €3.49 billion), the attackers exploited Ethereum Improvement Proposal (EIP) 7702 delegation.
Using 50 pre-signed authorisations prepared in advance, the perpetrators converted a Binance hot wallet into an automated sweeper contract directly under their control. TRM Labs said preparations had begun at least 36 hours before the theft.
Simultaneously, hot wallets across nine other networks began executing rapid, automated transfers to attacker-controlled addresses.
The outflows saw the extraction of approximately 200,630 ETH and 185 other tokens on Ethereum, including $1.875 billion in USDT, $823 million in USDC and $88.5 million in RLUSD.
On the Bitcoin network, 18,270 BTC worth approximately $1.47 billion (€1.35 billion) was drained, while on Tron, transfers accounted for 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX.
The operation also captured 233.46 million XRP from the XRP Ledger and 970,500 SOL on Solana, alongside multimillion-dollar balances across Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche and Polygon.
In the hours following the detection of the exploit, centralised stablecoin issuers and protocol administrators intervened to stem the flow of funds.
Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture backed by US President Donald Trump’s family, acted to freeze approximately $2.67 billion (€2.46 billion) in fiat-backed stablecoins across flagged recipient addresses. Tether moved first, at 9.01pm UTC, according to TRM Labs.
In parallel, the Arbitrum network’s Security Council intervened to immobilise 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB, bringing the total value of restricted or frozen funds to approximately $2.7 billion (€2.48 billion). Binance later put the frozen total at about $3 billion.
The perpetrators had anticipated administrative blacklisting, though.
While stablecoin issuers moved to halt transfers, the attackers executed rapid decentralised conversions, selling unblacklisted stablecoins into automated market makers and depositing tokens into lending protocols such as Aave to borrow native Ether, until Aave froze the affected markets.
As a result, TRM Labs reported that the hackers successfully converted and retained control over an estimated $2.4 billion (€2.21 billion) worth of unfreezable base assets, principally held in more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC.
Binance suspended withdrawals across multiple networks as security teams sought to isolate affected signing systems.
Binance co-founder and co-CEO Yi He issued a public statement confirming the breach, stating that deposits remained unaffected, the firm’s balance sheet would absorb all losses and user funds were fully backstopped through its emergency capital reserves, the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).
She said normal withdrawal operations were expected to resume within 48 hours.
A Binance spokesperson said the company was “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice”.
The scale of the incident reverberated through European and global trading desks on the morning of October 30.
Bitcoin fell by more than 3 per cent to $76,368 (€70,244), Ether declined 3.2 per cent to $2,178 (€2,003) and Binance’s native exchange token, BNB, shed roughly 5 per cent.
The breach comes as Binance faces scrutiny in the EU. The exchange did not secure a licence under the bloc’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) before the July 1 deadline and now serves European customers from its Abu Dhabi entity.
Regulators in France, Germany and Greece are examining its reliance on a “reverse solicitation” exemption to do so, the Financial Times reported on October 1.
Western intelligence officials and sanctions monitoring bodies have long flagged Pyongyang’s cyber apparatus as a primary financing pipeline for the regime’s illicit ballistic and nuclear weapons programmes.
Chainalysis estimated in December 2025 that North Korean hackers had stolen about $2 billion (€1.84 billion) in cryptocurrency that year, a record at the time.
European Union and United States authorities have reiterated that tracing efforts remain active through coordinated multilateral cyber defence networks.

sources.news_title: Crypto Platform Binance Confirms 'Complex' $6.3bn Hack
sources.text:
Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a “complex attack” that hit around $6.3 billion in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft.
The company — the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes — said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach”, contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.
The firm earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”
The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion.”
That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform.
Binance warned the figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”
It said around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
The 2023 Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor.
Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said Thursday it had “high confidence” that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing “robust on and off-chain intelligence.”
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group — which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for “The Interview,” a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Fund freeze
At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended”.
“Deposits remain unaffected,” it said.
The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorised party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
But it said later that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.”
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether — a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT — said his firm froze about $1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

sources.news_title: North Korean hackers steal over $6 billion from the largest cryptocurrency exchange
sources.text:
North Korean hackers steal over $6 billion from the largest cryptocurrency exchange
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Hackers from North Korea stole $6.3 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance.
Binance said they are working with law enforcement to solve the issue. An insider called it “the largest bank heist in human history,” according to the New York Post.
The exchange made it clear that deposits were not impacted by the hack and they are working with partners to freeze assets that were affected.
A US-based blockchain intelligence firm called TRM Labs pinned the attack on TraderTraitor, which is a North Korean hacking unit.
“We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm stated. It added that the attack is similar to other heists linked to North Korea.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM stated.
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said that the attack was complex and wasn’t done with one click.
“Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop,” he said, according to the BBC. “That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions."

sources.news_title: Binance Hack: Are Funds Safu? What We Know So Far
sources.text:
Binance Hack: Are Funds Safu? What We Know So Far About the Biggest Heist in Crypto History
